failures.title: Peugeot EP6 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch and Tensioner Failure
items.whatHappens: Early EP6 engines (particularly pre-2010 THP variants) are notorious for premature timing chain stretch and plastic guide degradation. This manifests as a distinct rattling noise on cold starts. If ignored, the chain can skip teeth, leading to catastrophic valve-to-piston contact and complete engine destruction.
items.repairVsReplace: While replacing the chain, guides, and tensioners is a viable repair if caught early, the labour intensity of the job means that if secondary damage has occurred, a full reconditioned Peugeot EP6 engine replacement is the only reliable fix.

items.title: High-Pressure Fuel Pump (HPFP) Failure
items.whatHappens: The direct-injection EP6 relies on a mechanically driven HPFP. Internal wear or seal failure can lead to a loss of fuel pressure, resulting in hard starting, rough idling, loss of power, and the illumination of the check engine light. In severe cases, fuel can dilute the engine oil, accelerating internal wear.
items.repairVsReplace: Replacing the HPFP is a standard repair. However, if fuel dilution has already caused bearing wear or if the failure was triggered by underlying timing issues, a comprehensive engine replacement is often the most financially sensible long-term solution.

items.title: Carbon Buildup on Intake Valves
items.whatHappens: Because the EP6 uses direct fuel injection, fuel does not wash over the intake valves to clean them. Over time, oil vapour from the PCV system combines with exhaust gases to form heavy carbon deposits. This restricts airflow, leading to misfires, hesitation, and reduced fuel economy.
items.repairVsReplace: Walnut blasting or chemical decarbonisation is a standard maintenance procedure. If left unaddressed for too long, the resulting performance degradation can mask or exacerbate other underlying engine faults.

failures.goodYearsLine: Post-2010 revisions of the EP6 saw updated timing chain guides, revised tensioners, and improved HPFP seals, making later THP units marginally more robust. However, the fundamental Prince architecture vulnerabilities remain, and strict adherence to manufacturer oil specifications is non-negotiable .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the EP6
variants.intro: As a Specific page type with no distinct sub-codes listed in the inventory, this section focuses on accurate identification and avoiding common, costly misidentifications. The EP6 engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the cylinder block and is also recorded on your vehicle’s V5C registration document under "Engine Number". Owners and breakers frequently confuse the EP6 with the newer PureTech family, such as the EB2ADT or EB2ADTS. While both are 1.6-litre or 1.2-litre turbocharged PSA engines, the EP6 is a fundamentally different architecture featuring a timing chain, a different block casting, and a distinct engine management system. The PureTech engines use a "wet" timing belt and a 3-cylinder layout. Additionally, the EP6 is often confused with the older, naturally aspirated TU5 1.6L engine. Fitting an EB2ADT wiring harness, ECU, or ancillary components to an EP6 host will result in incorrect fueling, persistent fault codes, and a non-running vehicle.

relatives.description: The - the outgoing 1.6-litre naturally aspirated engine that the EP6 replaced, offering a simpler, more robust architecture but with less low-end torque and refinement.
The - the updated 1.2-litre PureTech family that eventually replaced the EP6, offering improved thermal efficiency and a different (though still complex) wet-belt architecture.
the higher-output 1.6-litre THP variant (up to 175hp) found in performance models like the 308 GTi, featuring a larger turbocharger and revised ECU mapping.

The - the exact same "Prince" engine architecture co-developed by BMW and PSA, found in the Mini Cooper and BMW 1 Series, sharing the identical timing chain and high-pressure fuel pump vulnerabilities.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement EP6 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Peugeot EP6 engine for sale can be a viable, budget-friendly option for older 207 projects, but it carries a severe inherent risk. Unless the seller can provide documented proof that the timing chain and tensioners have been replaced recently with updated parts, and the HPFP is in good health, you are highly likely to be inheriting a ticking time bomb of chain stretch or fuel system degradation. Learn more about used engines.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: For most owners, a reconditioned Peugeot EP6 is the only sensible choice. A proper recon will proactively address the engine’s known weaknesses by fitting a brand-new, updated timing chain kit, replacing the tensioners, and verifying or replacing the HPFP, delivering peace of mind for the future. Explore reconditioned engine options.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for low-mileage 308 or 3008 projects where the engine is being stripped to the bare block. This allows for comprehensive decarbonisation of the intake valves, seal replacement, and verification of the turbocharger, ensuring the engine matches the pristine condition of the host chassis. View rebuilt engine services.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting your replacement through our vetted network ensures the work is completed by specialists familiar with PSA Prince engine systems and ECU adaptation, backed by a nationwide warranty. Check supply and fit availability.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Peugeot 207, 308, and 3008 models typically hold values between £1,500 and £8,000, depending heavily on age, mileage, and body condition . Because a fully fitted, reconditioned Peugeot EP6 engine replacement can approach £2,915, it is crucial to evaluate the vehicle's overall condition before committing to a major mechanical investment. Older 207 models valued under £3,000 frequently sit at the scrap threshold. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value first.

items.question: How much does a Peugeot EP6 engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned Peugeot EP6 engine typically costs between £1,200 and £2,200 for supply only, with fitted prices ranging from £1,720 to £2,915. Used units start around £400 but carry a severe risk of inherited timing chain or HPFP issues. Full rebuilt units can exceed £3,500 for comprehensive restoration specifications. items.question: What is the most common failure on the Peugeot EP6 engine?
items.answer: The most critical failure on the EP6 is timing chain stretch and tensioner failure, particularly in early (pre-2010) THP variants. High-pressure fuel pump (HPFP) failure is also prevalent, leading to hard starting and power loss. Heavy carbon buildup on intake valves is a known issue due to the direct injection design, restricting airflow and causing misfires.

items.question: Which Peugeot models use the EP6 engine?
items.answer: The EP6 1.6-litre turbo petrol engine was fitted to the Peugeot 207, 308, and 3008 between 2005 and 2015. It served as the primary mid-range petrol powerplant, offering strong low-end torque and improved fuel economy over older PSA engines. It was co-developed with BMW and is widely known as the "Prince" engine.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned EP6 engine?
items.answer: For any Peugeot 207, 308, or 3008, a reconditioned EP6 is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the high risk of timing chain and HPFP failure. Used engines almost always inherit the same stretched timing chain or failing fuel pump that caused the original removal. A proper reconditioned build proactively installs a brand-new, updated timing chain kit, replaces the tensioners, and verifies or replaces the HPFP. Reconditioned units also include comprehensive compression testing to guarantee reliability.

items.question: How do I know if my car has the EP6 engine?
items.answer: You can confirm your engine code by checking the V5C registration document under the "Engine Number" field or by locating the code stamped on the cylinder block. The EP6 is easily distinguished from the newer PureTech family (like the EB2ADT) by its timing chain drive (rather than a wet belt) and different block casting. Fitting an EB2ADT wiring harness or ECU to an EP6 host will result in incorrect fueling, persistent fault codes, and a non-running vehicle.
